section.title: Blessed Are Those Who Fear the Lord
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents, ninth in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Following Psalm 127's confession that the LORD alone builds the house, this psalm pictures the ordinary, flourishing life of the household built and blessed by Him.
section.thesis: Blessing rests on everyone who fears the LORD and walks in His ways, seen in fruitful labor, a flourishing family, and the wider peace of Zion, a blessing that flows from and is fulfilled in Christ, who perfectly feared the LORD and secures every spiritual blessing for His people.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the blessing of fruitful labor for the one who fears the LORD, verses 1 to 2, the blessing of a flourishing family, verses 3 to 4, and the closing blessing of peace from Zion for generations to come, verses 5 to 6.

units.label: Blessed are all who fear the LORD

verses.text: Blessed are all who {{yare|fear}} the LORD, who walk in His ways!
For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours.

units.label: A fruitful vine and olive shoots

verses.text: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house, your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table.
In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who {{yare|fears}} the LORD.
May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life,
that you may see your children's children. Peace be upon Israel!

yare.gloss: To fear, revere, stand in reverential awe; not terror but a whole-life submission to the LORD that shapes obedient walking in His ways, verses 1 and 4.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents pictures the ordinary blessings that flow from reverent obedience to the LORD, fruitful labor, a flourishing household, and generations to come, all set within the wider peace and prosperity of Zion.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes the blessed pattern of an Israelite household under the covenant, and it prescribes as an abiding truth that reverence for the LORD, walking in His ways, is the foundation of a genuinely flourishing life, whatever its particular circumstances.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens and closes its central section with yare, fear of the LORD, reverent awe that shapes obedient living, the same reverence Proverbs 1:7 calls the beginning of wisdom.
basic.typology: The fruitful vine within the house anticipates Christ, the true vine in whom His people abide and bear fruit, and the fear of the LORD perfectly embodied in this psalm's ideal man anticipates Christ, on whom the Spirit of the fear of the LORD rests without measure.
basic.christ: Isaiah 11:2-3 describes the coming Messiah as delighting in the fear of the LORD, the perfect fulfillment of the blessed man this psalm describes, and Jesus calls His people to abide in Him as the true vine, John 15:4-5, so that their lives bear the fruit this psalm celebrates.
basic.god: The LORD blesses reverent obedience with fruitful labor, a flourishing household, and the sight of generations to come, and He is the source of Zion's peace and prosperity that overflows into the life of every household that fears Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 11:2-3 pictures the Messiah delighting in the fear of the LORD. John 15:4-5 calls believers to abide in Christ, the true vine, to bear fruit. Ephesians 1:3 declares that God has blessed believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's picture of blessing flowing from the fear of the LORD is fulfilled in Christ, who perfectly feared and obeyed the Father, and in whom, as the true vine, His people are grafted to bear lasting fruit and receive every spiritual blessing.

context.literary:
The psalm moves in concentric circles. It begins with a person, 'all who fear the LORD', and in verse 2 narrows to a single worker at his table. Verse 3 widens to the household, wife and sons. Verse 4 returns to the man at the centre, and verses 5 and 6 widen again, to Jerusalem and to Israel. The blessing starts in the heart, passes through the field and the home, and ends at the city and the nation. Nothing in the order is accidental: a blessing that begins in reverence is meant to reach as far as the whole people of God.

The frame is a pair of statements about the one who fears the LORD, verse 1 and verse 4. The first is an exclamation in the plural, 'Blessed are all who fear the LORD'; the second is a declaration about a single man, 'blessing will come to the man who fears the LORD'. Between them, the speaker addresses the hearer as 'you', and the whole middle is a picture painted in the second person. The effect is of a priest or teacher speaking over each worshipper in turn.

Verses 5 and 6 change mood. Until then the psalm is a statement, 'blessed', 'will be yours'; here it becomes a wish, 'May the LORD bless you from Zion'. The grammar signals the change from observation to benediction. The wording is close to the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24 to 26, where the LORD is asked to bless and keep His people, and the last psalm of the Ascents ends with the same words: 'May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion', Psalm 134:3.

The images are pastoral. A vine is trained on a wall or trellis, olive shoots rise round the base of the parent tree, and a table is the centre of daily life. These are the three main crops of the land, grain, vine and olive, reduced to a family at a meal. The psalm ends with the same words that close Psalm 125, 'Peace be upon Israel', Psalm 125:5, so that the two psalms enclose the cluster of 126 to 127 with a common benediction.
context.historical:
The people who sang this psalm on the road to Jerusalem were mostly farmers and their households. The 'fruit of your labor' in verse 2 is the harvest of the plot they worked. In the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 a person could 'plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit' and watch 'a people you do not know' eat the produce of the land and 'all your toil', Deuteronomy 28:30 and 33. The psalm's picture is the opposite. The worker eats what he grows. That promise would have meant something very concrete to those who had seen their harvest taken by a foreign power, as the people of the exile had.

The ideal in verse 3 is a home within a village economy. The wife is not described as a worker or a decoration but as a vine, a source of fruit and shade, in the inner part of the house. The children are likened to olive shoots, which grow up from the base of an old tree and will in time take its place. The household sits round one table, a mark of security in a world where bread could be scarce. It is a picture of abundance in the small, daily scale a common family could recognise.

The reference to 'the prosperity of Jerusalem' in verse 5 reflects a pilgrim's perspective. The Songs of Ascents were sung on the way to Jerusalem, and pilgrims prayed for the peace of the city, Psalm 122:6 to 8. The household blessing is bound up with the welfare of the holy city, because the LORD's blessing is said to come 'from Zion', where His house stood. The man who fears the LORD in his own village is part of a nation whose centre is the place where the LORD is worshipped.

The picture of the grandchildren in verse 6 speaks to a culture in which a long line of descendants was the chief earthly hope. Joseph saw his great-grandchildren, Genesis 50:23, and Job lived to see four generations, Job 42:16. Proverbs says 'Grandchildren are the crown of the aged', Proverbs 17:6. To see them was the sign of a full life.

Seen against exile, the psalm is also a hope. A people driven from home could pray these words about a future they had not yet been given, and the prophets promised the same picture of building, planting and eating one's own fruit, Isaiah 65:21 to 23.
context.canonical:
The psalm is a close companion of Psalm 1, which opens the Psalter with a man who is 'blessed', who delights in the Law, and who is 'like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season', Psalm 1:1 to 3. Psalm 128 sets that tree in a household. Psalm 112 begins 'Blessed is the man who fears the LORD' and promises that his descendants will be mighty in the land, Psalm 112:1 and 2, and Psalm 144:12 to 15 speaks of sons like plants and ends 'Blessed are the people whose God is the LORD'.

The fear of the LORD is the foundation of wisdom writing. 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge', Proverbs 1:7, and 'the beginning of wisdom', Proverbs 9:10 and Psalm 111:10. Ecclesiastes ends on it: 'Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man', Ecclesiastes 12:13. Proverbs 14:26 says that 'he who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge', which is a prose version of what this psalm sings.

The prophets pick up the picture of fruitful ordinary life. Isaiah 65:21 to 23 promises a time when people build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and 'will not labor in vain or bear children doomed to disaster'. Hosea 14:5 and 6 speaks of Israel blossoming, with shoots that sprout and splendour like the olive tree.

The New Testament reads the household blessing in Christ. Jesus calls Himself the true vine, John 15:1 to 5, and says the Father is glorified when His disciples bear much fruit, John 15:8. Paul speaks of the fruit of the Spirit, Galatians 5:22 and 23, and says God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing', Ephesians 1:3. Romans 11:17 describes believers from the nations as a wild olive shoot grafted into the olive root. The psalm's images of vine and olive, with their roots in the earth of Israel, become images of the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist is teaching a worshipping people what a good life under God looks like, in a form simple enough to be sung on the road. He is not a prosperity preacher. He points the hearer toward ordinary things, a meal one has earned, a household that gathers, children who grow, a city at peace, and tells them that these are gifts to be received with reverence.

The structure of the psalm makes the point that what holds these gifts together is the fear of the LORD. It is mentioned at the start and again at verse 4, as the condition that makes every other line true. The audience is meant to hear that blessing is a relationship before it is a result.

He also means to widen their sight. The last two verses move from the household to Zion and to Israel, and they ask the hearer to look past the family table. The man who sits among his sons is asked to care for Jerusalem's welfare and for the future of the people to come, so that private blessing becomes a share in a public one. The psalm ends with a prayer for peace on all Israel, which is the author's way of saying that no family flourishes in isolation from the people of God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes the shape of a blessed life in the language of ancient agriculture and household. It describes more than it commands. Its single imperative-like note is in the first verse, to fear the LORD and walk in His ways, and the rest says what follows from that. The details of wife, sons, table and long life belong to the world of the psalm, and they cannot be turned into a checklist for every believer's home.

The psalm should also be read with the rest of Scripture's account of the godly. Job was blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil, and he lost his children and his health, Job 1:1. Ecclesiastes 7:15 observes a righteous man perishing in his righteousness. Jesus tells His followers that those who leave home and family for the kingdom will receive many times more in this age, but also persecutions, and in the age to come, eternal life, Luke 18:29 and 30. A proverb of blessing describes the pattern God has built into His world and does not state a law that applies without exception.

What carries forward as instruction is the root. Reverence for the LORD, shown in walking in His ways, is the ground of a good life, and the person who has it can receive both prosperity and its absence with a steady heart, as Habakkuk does, Habakkuk 3:17 and 18. The psalm also invites believers to see their own ordinary bread and family as gifts.

debates.question: Does the psalm promise material prosperity and family blessing to everyone who fears the LORD?

views.label: A covenant pattern under the Mosaic order
views.case: The psalm follows the shape of the blessings of Deuteronomy 28, where obedience brings fruitful fields, fruit of the womb and security, Deuteronomy 28:1 to 6. On this reading the psalm speaks to Israel under the covenant, in a time when such blessings were tied visibly to faithfulness, and Christians read it in the light of Christ rather than as a direct promise.

views.label: A proverb about how God's world generally works
views.case: Wisdom literature states patterns, not guarantees. Job, Ecclesiastes 7:15 and Psalm 73:13 and 14 show faithful people who suffer, and the psalm sits in a Psalter that knows this. Habakkuk can rejoice in the LORD with empty fields, Habakkuk 3:17 and 18, and Paul says godliness is valuable in every way, 'holding promise for the present life and for the one to come', 1 Timothy 4:8.

debates.bearing: Both views refuse to turn the psalm into a bargain with God. The practical result is gratitude for what is given and steadiness when it is withheld. The final blessing is in Christ, Ephesians 1:3, who gives every spiritual blessing.

debates.question: Is the psalm only about men, since it addresses 'the man who fears the LORD' and speaks of his wife and sons?

views.label: It addresses a male head of household, but sets a pattern for all
views.case: The language reflects the ancient household, in which the husband was the one who worked the land and spoke at the gate. The reverent person is described as a man because the household is. The principle of fearing the LORD is for everyone, and Scripture says elsewhere that 'a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised', Proverbs 31:30.

views.label: It is a specific, culturally bound portrait that should not be extended
views.case: Others hold that the picture of a wife as a vine and sons around the table is too tied to its time to be applied directly. The details are an image of fullness and not a model of roles, and attention should rest on the central claim, that blessing flows from the fear of the LORD.

debates.bearing: The psalm's centre is not the shape of the household but the person who fears the LORD. Every believer, man or woman, married or single, with children or without, can take the first and last words of the psalm for their own: blessed are all who fear the LORD, and peace be upon Israel.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for 'blessed' in verse 1 is ashre, a plural construct that means something like 'the happinesses of'. It is a different word from the one used of God's act of blessing, barak, which appears in verses 4 and 5. Ashre is the word that opens Psalm 1 and names the state of a person whose life is in order; barak is what God does to bestow good. The psalm joins both: those who live in the first condition are in the line of the second action. In verse 2 the Hebrew has 'happy are you, and it will be well with you', two short phrases the BSB renders as 'blessings and prosperity'.

The fear of the LORD, yirat Adonai, is the reverence due to a holy and generous God. The verb yare, 'fear', ranges from terror to awe. In the wisdom and covenant tradition it is the right response to a God who has acted, Exodus 14:31, and it is joined with walking in His ways, Deuteronomy 10:12. The psalm combines them at once: 'fear the LORD, who walk in His ways'. The two phrases are an explanation of each other. Fear is the attitude, and walking is the shape it takes in daily life.

The phrase in verse 2, 'the fruit of your labor', literally uses the word for the 'work of your palms' or 'the toil of your hands', a physical expression for hard labour. The verb 'eat' is the key, because the whole verse is about being able to eat what one has made. It reverses the sentence of Genesis 3:17 to 19, where the man eats 'through toil' and 'by the sweat of your brow', and it reverses the covenant curse of having others eat one's produce. The toil remains, but the toil is now fruitful and the fruit is enjoyed.

The images of verse 3 are botanical, and the Hebrew words give them texture. The vine is called fruitful, and the verse places her 'within your house', in a phrase the BSB renders simply and that points toward the inner part of the home. The sons are 'olive shoots', shetilim, a word for young plants set out and tended. They are 'around your table', a phrase that pictures them in a ring, like shoots round the base of an olive tree. The olive was a long-lived tree and a staple crop, so the image is of continuity.

The word for 'man' in verse 4 is geber, which is a different word from the more general 'adam' or the common 'ish'. It means a man in his strength, a man as head of the household or a mighty man. It underlines that the strong person described in the psalm is blessed by fear of the LORD, not by his strength. The closing 'Peace be upon Israel' is shalom al-Yisrael, the wish that ends Psalm 125 and that Paul turns to the church in Galatians 6:16, 'Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God'.

typology.type: The fruitful vine within the house, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: In the Old Testament Israel is the LORD's vine, brought out of Egypt and planted, Psalm 80:8 and 9, and the prophets mourn that it brought forth bad fruit, Isaiah 5:7. The household vine of Psalm 128 is a small picture of that larger fruitfulness. Jesus says, 'I am the true vine', John 15:1, and the branches that remain in Him bear fruit. The correspondence rises from a family to a people joined to one person, and from an earthly harvest to the fruit of the Spirit, Galatians 5:22 and 23. The type falls short because a household vine can be cut off or fail, whereas union with Christ is held by the Father, the keeper of the vineyard.

typology.type: The man who fears the LORD, verses 1 and 4
typology.fulfillment: The blessed man of the Psalter is a figure who awaits a perfect instance. Isaiah promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse who will delight in the fear of the LORD, Isaiah 11:1 to 3, and the New Testament shows Him as one who 'learned obedience from what He suffered' and was heard 'because of His reverence', Hebrews 5:7 and 8. He is the one person who feared the LORD without any failure. The type falls short because every other fearer of the LORD is flawed and receives blessing as a gift; Christ receives the blessing as of right and gives it to others.

typology.type: Olive shoots round the table, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The olive was Israel's emblem of lasting fruitfulness, Jeremiah 11:16 and Hosea 14:6. Paul takes up the olive tree in Romans 11:17 and 18, saying that Gentile believers, like wild shoots, have been grafted into the root of Israel's blessing, and that the root supports them. The sons round the table become a family of those joined to the Messiah by faith. Jesus' table in the upper room is the greater gathering, and the Lord's Supper is the table the church shares, 1 Corinthians 10:16 and 17. The type is partial, since a family table is limited to one generation and one household, while Christ's table is as wide as the nations.

The LORD blesses from Zion, the place of His dwelling. The church is told that it has come to 'Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem', Hebrews 12:22. The blessing sent out from Zion finds its fullest form in Christ, who is raised and seated in glory, from whom the Spirit comes, Acts 2:33. The type is imperfect because the earthly Jerusalem could be besieged, whereas the heavenly one is the city that cannot be shaken, Hebrews 12:28.

study.christ:
The psalm's central figure is the person who fears the LORD, and no one fits that description as Jesus does. Isaiah says of the coming Shoot that the Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him, the Spirit of 'knowledge and fear of the LORD', and that 'He will delight in the fear of the LORD', Isaiah 11:2 and 3. The Gospels show it: He grew 'in favor with God and man', Luke 2:52, and Hebrews says that He was heard 'because of His reverence' and 'learned obedience from what He suffered', Hebrews 5:7 and 8. The man who walks in all the ways of the LORD, in the psalm's first line, is realised in Him alone.

The blessing comes to others through Him. It is not our fear that earns anything. Paul writes that God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms', Ephesians 1:3. What the psalm shows in the shape of an Israelite household, the New Testament holds out as the gift of union with the Son. The curse of toil in Genesis 3 is answered in the life to come, where those who die in the Lord 'rest from their labors', Revelation 14:13.

The vine is His own metaphor. 'I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard', John 15:1. The psalm gives a picture of a wife as a fruitful vine, and Jesus applies the picture to the people He gathers: 'Remain in Me, and I will remain in you', John 15:4. In a household the vine is fruitful because it is rooted; in Christ believers are fruitful because they are in Him. The Father is glorified when they bear much fruit, John 15:8.

The sons round the table suggest a family gathered in peace. Jesus makes His followers a family, saying that whoever does the will of His Father is His brother and sister and mother, Matthew 12:50, and Hebrews says that He is not ashamed to call them brothers, Hebrews 2:11. He eats with His disciples at a table, and promises to eat again with them in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 26:29.

The final wish of the psalm, 'Peace be upon Israel', meets its fulfilment in the one who 'is our peace', Ephesians 2:14, who made Jew and Gentile into one new man and proclaimed peace to those far and near, Ephesians 2:17. The Israel of God, Galatians 6:16, is the community He has made, and the benediction of the psalm is spoken over it.

The reading needs restraint. The psalm is about households and fields, and it does not mention a Messiah. It would be wrong to find Christ in the number of the sons or the wife's role. The connections depend on the images that the New Testament itself uses, the vine, the olive, the fear of the LORD, the blessing from Zion, and on the way Jesus fulfils what those images stand for.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who blesses the ordinary. There is no miracle in it and no battle, only a meal, a home and a family growing up. He is not a God who limits His attention to temples and sacrifices; He attends to the person who eats at the end of a day's work. The psalm turns the table into a place where His goodness is seen, and it shows that His care covers bread and children, health and peace.

He is a God who ties blessing to a relationship. The psalm opens with a person who fears Him and walks in His ways and places blessing on that foundation. The LORD is not an impersonal source of good outcomes. He gives good to those who stand in right relation to Him, and the right relation is reverent obedience, which Deuteronomy 10:12 describes as walking in His ways and loving Him. The same God who is feared is the God who gives, so that fear and trust are not opposites in the psalm.

He is a God of order. The sequence of the blessings, work, wife, children, city, nation, reflects a world He has made with a pattern. The pattern is the same as the creation mandate of Genesis 1:28, to be fruitful, to fill and to work. The psalm delights in the rightness of that order, and it assumes that He wants His creatures to enjoy it.

He is also a God who blesses from a place. The blessing comes 'from Zion', where He chose to dwell, Psalm 132:13. The psalm sees no conflict between His transcendence and His presence among His people. Psalm 134:3 calls Him 'the Maker of heaven and earth' who blesses from Zion, which says the same thing in one sentence.

The psalm leaves an honest tension. A God who blesses reverence is also the God who permits Job's loss and Israel's exile. The psalm does not resolve it by explaining suffering. It describes what He normally gives and what He will finally give, and it leaves room for the rest of Scripture to speak of the cost of faithfulness. A reader should keep both truths: that He is good to those who fear Him, and that His goodness is larger than what is visible in any one life.

For worship, the psalm teaches that gratitude for daily bread and family is a form of reverence. A person who prays over a meal, who thanks God for children and grandchildren, who prays for the welfare of the city, is practising this psalm. It also teaches the community to bless one another in the LORD's name, as the closing verses do, and to wish peace on the whole people of God.

crossReferences.note: The opening psalm describes a blessed man who delights in the Law and is like a tree planted by streams, yielding fruit in its season. Psalm 128 translates that single tree into a household of vine and shoots. Both use the same word for blessed and both link fruit to a life ordered by the LORD.

The covenant blessings promise blessing in the city and country, in the fruit of the womb and the produce of the land. Psalm 128 reads like a song version of these verses. It shows how the covenant promises were meant to be felt in an ordinary home, and why the exile, which reversed them, was so painful.

Moses asks what the LORD requires: to fear Him by walking in all His ways, to love Him and to serve Him with all the heart. The pairing of fear and walking in verse 1 of the psalm comes from here. The psalm shows what the life that Moses describes looks like when it is lived.

The priestly blessing asks the LORD to bless and keep His people, to make His face shine on them and to give them peace. Verses 5 and 6 of the psalm echo it closely, in the wish for blessing and in the closing word of peace. The household psalm ends in the priests' language.

The final Song of Ascents closes with the words 'May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion'. The wording matches Psalm 128:5, and together they frame the collection of pilgrim songs. The blessing that began on the road is the blessing the pilgrim carries home.

In the new heavens and earth the LORD's people will build and dwell, plant and eat, and will not labour in vain or bear children doomed to disaster. It promises the picture of Psalm 128 in its fullest form, with work that lasts and descendants who are blessed, so that the psalm is read as a foretaste.

The prophet rejoices in the LORD though the fig tree does not bud, the vines are bare and the olive crop fails. It is a necessary companion to Psalm 128, because it shows faith that does not depend on the blessings the psalm describes, and so protects the psalm from being read as a guarantee.

Jesus promises that those who have left home or family for the kingdom will receive many times more in this age and eternal life in the age to come. It reframes the household of Psalm 128 in Christ: the blessing may be received through the new family of the church, and it is guaranteed in the age to come.

Jesus calls Himself the true vine and His disciples the branches that bear fruit only when they remain in Him. It takes the psalm's vine and makes it the picture of life in Christ, so that fruitfulness is no longer a matter of family fortune but of union with Him.

Paul opens his letter with praise to the Father who, in the Son, has already given His people all the good that belongs to the heavenly places. This is the New Testament form of what the psalm sings, lifted from fields and table to gifts that cannot be lost.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a blessing. God blesses the first man and woman and tells them to be fruitful, to fill the earth and to work it, Genesis 1:28. Psalm 128 is one of the clearest pictures in the Psalter of that blessing at home in ordinary life. It shows what the creation mandate was meant to look like: work that feeds, a household that grows, a table that gathers, and peace for the city.

The fall spoiled each part of it. Work became toil, Genesis 3:17 to 19, the bearing of children became painful, and the family was set against itself. The psalm is a song from within that broken world that nevertheless sees the blessing returning. It does not deny the thorns. It insists that the LORD gives good to those who fear Him and that the first purpose of creation is not lost.

The promise to Abraham is the thread that carries the blessing forward. He is promised descendants and a land and that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him and his offspring, Genesis 28:14. The covenant blessings of Deuteronomy 28 spell it out for the nation, and the exile is the reversal of them. The psalm is sung by a people who know the blessing and the loss and who ask for it again from Zion.

In Christ the blessing is restored at its root. He is the true vine and the one who feared the LORD perfectly, and in Him the blessing of Abraham comes to the nations, Galatians 3:14. His people are a new family, gathered at one table and given every spiritual blessing. They bear fruit in Him now, and they wait for the day when the toil is over, when the peace of Jerusalem is complete and the saints see the full promise of Isaiah 65.

The new creation is the household psalm at its largest. The city comes down from God, and the LORD dwells with His people, Revelation 21:2 and 3. The tree of life stands by the river, bearing its fruit, Revelation 22:2. The vine is fruitful, the table is spread, and the sons and daughters of God see 'your children's children' in a family that has no end. Peace is upon Israel, the Israel of God, for ever.

sermon.title: Count Your Blessings
sermon.why: Begg treats Psalms 126 to 128 together, showing how this psalm's picture of a flourishing household under the fear of the LORD completes the sequence's teaching on God's blessing of ordinary life.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, who is called blessed?

options.text: All who fear the LORD and walk in His ways.
options.note: This is the exact condition of blessing the psalm names at the outset.

options.text: Only those born into wealthy families.
options.note: The psalm ties blessing to reverence and obedience, not birth or wealth.

options.text: Anyone who works hard, regardless of their relationship to God.
options.note: The psalm specifically ties blessing to fearing the LORD, not mere hard work alone.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The blessing described is for any person who fears the LORD, not a priestly class alone.

quiz.q: What does verse 2 say results from eating the fruit of your labor?

options.text: Blessings and prosperity will be yours.
options.note: This is the exact promise attached to fruitful labor for the one who fears the LORD.

options.text: Endless anxiety about the future.
options.note: The psalm promises blessing and prosperity, the opposite of anxiety.

options.text: A guarantee of never working again.
options.note: The verse assumes ongoing labor whose fruit is blessed, not the cessation of work.

options.text: Immediate exemption from all hardship.
options.note: The psalm promises blessing on labor, not a blanket exemption from every hardship.

quiz.q: How does verse 3 picture the wife and children of the one who fears the LORD?

options.text: A fruitful vine within the house and olive shoots around the table.
options.note: These are the exact images the psalm uses for a flourishing family.

options.text: A barren field and empty table.
options.note: The psalm's images are of fruitfulness and abundance, the opposite of barrenness.

options.text: A distant relationship with little contact.
options.note: The image is intimate and flourishing, gathered around the table, not distant.

options.text: A source of constant conflict.
options.note: The psalm's picture is one of flourishing and joy, not conflict.

quiz.q: What does the psalm pray for in verses 5 to 6 regarding Zion and generations?

options.text: That the LORD would bless from Zion and grant sight of children's children, with peace upon Israel.
options.note: This is the exact content of the closing prayer and blessing.

options.text: That Zion's prosperity would end within the reader's lifetime.
options.note: The prayer is for prosperity to continue all the days of one's life, not to end.

options.text: That the reader would leave Jerusalem permanently.
options.note: The prayer is for seeing Jerusalem's ongoing prosperity, not for leaving it.

options.text: That only the reader's generation would be blessed, with no future generations in view.
options.note: The prayer explicitly includes seeing one's children's children, future generations.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament deepen this psalm's picture of a fruitful vine?

options.text: Jesus calls believers to abide in Him as the true vine so that they bear lasting fruit.
options.note: John 15:4-5 takes up the vine imagery and applies it to union with Christ.

options.text: It rejects vine imagery as belonging only to the old covenant.
options.note: Jesus explicitly uses this very vine imagery of Himself and His disciples.

options.text: It applies the vine only to literal agriculture, never to spiritual life.
options.note: John 15 applies the vine directly to spiritual union with Christ, not mere agriculture.

options.text: It teaches that fruitfulness now depends entirely on human effort alone.
options.note: John 15 teaches that fruit comes from abiding in Christ, not from unaided human effort.

questions: The psalm ties blessing to fearing the LORD and walking in His ways. What would it look like this week to let reverence for God shape an ordinary decision you face?

The psalm pictures a flourishing household as a fruit of God's blessing. Whether or not your own family looks like this picture, how do you see God's fruitfulness at work in your life and relationships?
The prayer widens from personal blessing to the peace of the whole people of God. Who beyond your own household are you praying for God to bless and keep in peace?
Jesus calls His people to abide in Him as the true vine in order to bear fruit. Where do you need to depend more on Christ rather than your own effort to produce lasting fruit in your life?
The psalm ends by looking toward future generations, children's children. What are you doing now to plant faith and blessing that will outlast your own lifetime?

translationNotes.note: Fear of the LORD, yare, denotes reverential awe leading to obedience, the same disposition Proverbs 1:7 calls the beginning of wisdom, not mere terror.
Olive shoots around the table pictures young olive saplings growing beside a mature tree, an image of vigorous new life gathered close to its source.
Bless you from Zion locates the source of personal blessing in the LORD's chosen dwelling place, tying individual flourishing to the wider life and worship of God's people.
